text: A 20-minute research vision for retrieval, memory, continual learning, evaluation, and sequencing

text:
Open by saying that ARIA should not be treated as a single predictive model.
The core thesis: ARIA is an evidence-grounded memory system that retrieves, updates, and explains prior experience as the archive evolves.

[Sources] Research vision exercise prompt: /Users/akahmad/Downloads/Research Vison Exercise.docx
The hard problem is not prediction alone
textPreview: The hard problem is not prediction alone

text: ARIA must reason over a living clinical archive where evidence is heterogeneous, incomplete, temporal, and continuously changing.
textPreview: ARIA must reason over a living clinical archive where evidence is heterogeneous, incomplete, temporal, and continuously changing.

text: Retrieve relevant evidence, not just similar records
textPreview: Retrieve relevant evidence, not just similar records

text: Update memory without forgetting or drifting silently

text: Explain answers through traceable archive evidence
textPreview: Explain answers through traceable archive evidence

text:
Use this slide to define the tension. If ARIA only optimizes predictive accuracy, it misses the archive use case.
The system needs to support multiple biomedical tasks by making evidence retrievable and auditable.

Emphasize separation of concerns: data ingestion, representation, retrieval, and updates can evolve independently.

The phrase to remember: new evidence enters retrieval quickly; model behavior changes slowly.

Evaluation cadence: retrieval indexes can be evaluated weekly or monthly; representation/model updates should be gated by stronger retrospective tests.
